objective: Coordinator's go-ahead (18 November 2026) on TOUCH-CENSUS-20261118-001's direction 1: under the fewest counts, seven rings of five parity knots with five-place knots grew faster than any power with no chain of offshoots born. Prove the per-round growth of the ring of four four-place knots and one five-place knot, stopping at a proof of exponential growth or of a polynomial; say what the ring does that a chain cannot. Then, if this closes quickly, the plus-one rule when separately born chains combine (TOUCH-CENSUS #2). Serves G17, G2 and G1.
status: Complete 2026-11-18 (Successful; referee pending): under the cheapest counts the ring of four four-place knots and one five-place knot grows exponentially, c(t) = c(t-5) + c(t-6), rate 1.1347: the five-place knot's spare distinction opens one more independent direction on the cone above it, and on a ring that cone comes back over itself every lap, each lap adding a new direction (the advisor's (v, S) model; the count proved, the identification proved in outline and checked exactly to round 20). Rings of seven and eight follow the predicted recurrences; with j spare distinctions on a ring of n the rate is the root of x^(n+j) = (1+x)^j (the golden ratio for five five-place knots).
stop_rule: A proof of the growth rate (or of a polynomial), a computed check, referee hand-off, report.
title: Why do rings of five knots grow faster than any power under the cheapest counts?
